  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }

    - click: "Push: more"
    - click: "Push: more"
    - click: "Push: more"

In everyday talk "accelerate" means speed up. In physics it means something more exact.

## Engage: fast or accelerating?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students who equate acceleration with speed will choose the fast cruising car; the graph shows acceleration as change, not speed."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Which has the bigger acceleration: a car cruising at a steady 100 km/h, or a cyclist going from 0 to 20 km/h in 4 seconds?"
  options: ["The car, because it is much faster", "The cyclist, because their speed is changing", "Both the same", "Neither has any acceleration"]
  actual: "The cyclist. The car's speed isn't changing, so its acceleration is zero, however fast it goes. Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes."
```

## Explore: read the graph

```step
stage: run
insight: "Watching a straight-line speed–time graph build up, with the acceleration read out, links the gradient to a rate before the formula appears."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#speedup", height: 640 }
check: { type: board, text: "Run the trolley with a 6 N push for at least 4 seconds.", when: "t >= 4 and P = 6" }
```

Press **Play**. Watch how much the speed goes up each second (the graph and the numbers under it).

## Explain: a = Δv ÷ Δt

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Calculating acceleration from data, then giving it a direction, turns the everyday word into a defined vector quantity."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "The trolley went from 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s. What was its acceleration, in m/s²?"
      answer: 3
      explain: "a = change in velocity ÷ time = (12 − 0) ÷ 4 = 3 m/s². Its speed went up by 3 m/s every second."
    hint: ["How much did the speed go up altogether, and how many seconds did that take?", "Acceleration is the change in speed for each second, and the heading of this part of the lesson shows how to work it out."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "On the speed–time graph, where can you see the acceleration?"
      options: ["The gradient (steepness) of the line", "How high the line is", "Where the line ends"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Height is the speed at that moment, not how fast it changes.", "The end shows the final speed and time."]
      explain: "A steeper line means the speed changes faster: bigger acceleration. A flat line means zero acceleration."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What are the units of acceleration?"
      options: ["m/s² (metres per second, per second)", "m/s", "N", "km/h"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "m/s is velocity. Acceleration is how many m/s are added each second.", "N is force.", "km/h is a speed."]
    hint: "Acceleration counts how much speed gets added and how long that takes, so its unit has to carry both of those."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "A cyclist goes from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration, in m/s²?"
      answer: 2
      explain: "(10 − 2) ÷ 4 = 2 m/s²."
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is it accelerating?"
      options: ["Accelerating", "Not accelerating"]
      items:
        - ["A car cruising at a steady 100 km/h on a straight road", "Not accelerating", "Fast, but its velocity isn't changing."]
        - ["A bike slowing down for traffic lights", "Accelerating", "Slowing down is acceleration, opposite to the motion."]
        - ["A runner rounding a bend at a steady speed", "Accelerating", "Its direction changes, so its velocity changes."]
        - ["A trolley speeding up from rest", "Accelerating"]
        - ["A parked car", "Not accelerating"]
    hint: ["For each one, ask whether its velocity is changing, not whether it's fast.", "Speeding up isn't the only kind of change, so look for anything about the motion that's different from a moment ago."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A trolley is moving to the right, and the net force on it points to the left. Which way does its acceleration point?"
      options: ["Left, the same way as the net force", "Right, the way it is moving", "Nowhere: it has no acceleration while it still moves right"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Acceleration follows the net force, not the motion. Moving right while accelerating left means slowing down.", "Its velocity is changing (it is slowing down), so it is accelerating."]
      explain: "Acceleration always points the same way as the net force. Here that is backwards, so the trolley slows down."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained the difference between speed and acceleration, and how to calculate acceleration." }
```

In your book: explain why a car cruising at 100 km/h has zero acceleration, and a car pulling away from traffic lights has some.

## Elaborate: slowing down

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "A negative acceleration (opposite to the motion) shows acceleration as a direction, not just 'more speed'."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#slowdown", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Let the moving trolley slow to a stop.", when: "t >= 1 and v = 0" }
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "It went from 8 m/s to 0 in 4 s. What was its acceleration, in m/s²? (Use a minus sign for slowing down.)"
      answer: -2
      explain: "(0 − 8) ÷ 4 = −2 m/s². The minus sign means the acceleration points backwards, opposite to the motion, the same way as the net force (friction)."
    hint: "Take the starting speed away from the final speed to get the change, and keep whatever sign that gives you."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which way did the net force point while it slowed down?"
      options: ["Backwards, the same way as the acceleration", "Forwards, the way it was moving", "There was no net force"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Forwards would speed it up.", "Its speed changed, so there was a net force: friction."]
      explain: "Acceleration always points the same way as the net force."
```

## Elaborate: turning

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "A constant-speed turn is acceleration with no change of speed, the hardest case for 'acceleration = speeding up'."
check:
  type: question
  q: "A car drives around a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h. Is it accelerating?"
  options: ["Yes: its direction is changing, so its velocity is changing", "No: its speed is constant", "Only if it speeds up"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Velocity includes direction. A change of direction is a change of velocity.", "Speeding up is one kind; turning is another."]
  explain: "There must be a net force towards the centre of the roundabout: the friction of the tyres on the road."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the cruising car and the cyclist with what I now know." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: **a = Δv ÷ Δt**, in **m/s²**.
- It has a **direction**, the same as the net force. Slowing down is acceleration opposite to the motion (negative).
- A fast object at a steady speed has **zero** acceleration.
- On a speed–time graph of motion in a straight line, acceleration is the **gradient**. (Going round a bend at steady speed is still acceleration, because the direction changes.)

```teacher
summary: Students define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity,
  calculate it from data and graphs in m/s², and treat it as a vector in the
  direction of the net force (AC9S10U05, node 3, a hinge node).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 7 min · Explain 9 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds
  5 min, Wider about 2 min
goals:
  - I can define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity, in m/s².
  - I can calculate acceleration from velocity and time data, and read it from a
    speed–time graph.
  - I can explain that acceleration has a direction, the same as the net force;
    slowing down is acceleration too.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  motion sensors or ticker timers. Set the width with `?width=minimum`,
  `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  The hinge is the shift from the everyday word to a defined quantity. Keep
  separating "fast" from "changing speed".


  Board notes: the board's acceleration reading appears under the board, so the
  number checks use different numbers from the board where possible. The
  slowing-down board uses friction 4 N on 2 kg: a = −2 m/s².
running:
  - "Engage: ask why the cruising car isn't accelerating. Most will say it is."
  - "Explore: pause at 1, 2 and 3 seconds and read the speed: +3 m/s each time."
  - "Explain: insist on units for every answer aloud."
  - "In your own words: the cruising-car explanation is the evidence."
struggle: Separating acceleration (change in velocity) from speed. When a
  student says a fast car has a big acceleration, ask whether its speed is
  changing.
stuck:
  - see: A student says a fast car has big acceleration.
    ask: Is its speed changing?
    fix: No, so its acceleration is zero. Acceleration is the change, not the speed.
  - see: A student gives acceleration in m/s.
    ask: How much speed is added, and in how long?
    fix: "m/s added per second: m/s²."
  - see: A student says slowing down isn't acceleration.
    ask: Is the velocity changing?
    fix: Yes, so it's accelerating, backwards (negative).
stretch: A ball thrown straight up slows down, stops for an instant, then falls.
  What is its acceleration at the very top?
support: "Give the formula card: a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time, with
  one worked example."
leads: >
  Next: F = ma (node 4), which links the acceleration to the net force and the
  mass.


  In class: a motion sensor and a trolley on a ramp, or a ticker timer.
exit:
  q: A sprinter goes from 0 to 9 m/s in 3 s. What is her acceleration?
  a: a = (9 − 0) ÷ 3 = 3 m/s², forwards.
explain: >
  **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: a = Δv ÷ Δt, in m/s². It
  points the same way as the net force; slowing down is acceleration backwards.


  On a speed–time graph, acceleration is the gradient. A steady speed means zero
  acceleration, however fast.
```
